fact: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is known to spread both in a cell-free state and from cell to cell.
Design of vaccines attempts to inhibit HIV entry into target cells as do engineered entry inhibitors used as therapeutics.
Neutralizing antibodies and inhibitors block the entry of cell-free HIV particles into cells.
The activity of neutralizing antibodies and inhibitors during cell-cell transmission varies depending on their mode of action.

A prominent class of neutralizing antibodies directed to the CD4 binding site on the HIV envelope very efficiently blocks binding of the virus to its primary receptor on target cells, the CD4 molecule.
Neutralizing antibodies directed to the CD4 binding site on the HIV envelope are elicited in natural infection and once isolated from infected individuals have shown to be highly potent.

CD4 binding site antibodies are dramatically less potent inhibitors of HIV cell-cell transmission and therefore act preferentially by blocking free virus transmission while allowing HIV to spread through cell-cell contact.
Filarial nematodes are a group of pathogenic helminth parasites that include those responsible for the diseases lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis.
Filarial nematodes have evolved a mutualistic association with the intracellular bacterial symbiont Wolbachia, providing a novel approach to their treatment and control using antibiotics.
Depletion of Wolbachia leads to a rapid and sustained induction of cell death through apoptosis of reproductive cells, developing embryos, microfilariae, and developing larvae in filarial nematodes.
Apoptosis affects embryonic cells other than those infected with Wolbachia in filarial nematodes.
The Wolbachia populations in the adult hypodermis, rather than the few bacteria present in the developing embryos, are essential to avoid apoptosis in filarial nematodes.
The mode of action of antibiotic treatment of filarial nematodes includes induction of apoptosis due to depletion of Wolbachia, which accounts for some of the key anti-filarial activities.
American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) can lead to death in 5-10% of patients under treatment in Latin America.
The fatality rates associated with American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) have remained stable at a high level over the years in Brazil.
Fatality rates associated with American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) are not recorded in under-treatment patients from endemic countries of the Old World.
Fatality rates associated with American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) are not recorded in under-treatment patients from non-endemic countries where such cases are imported.
American visceral leishmaniasis (VL)-induced lethality can occur even after the implementation of recommended therapy.

Understanding individual, clinical, and laboratory factors that predispose to an unfavorable outcome might represent an important feature for informing better practice in the clinical management of American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) cases.
The present systematic review with meta-analysis brings together information on various prognostic variables associated with the severity of American visceral leishmaniasis (VL).

Potential predictors identified in the studies surveyed were grouped according to the strength of evidence available, and 13 were considered to be of significant relevance for American visceral leishmaniasis (VL).
There are gaps in the existing knowledge and a need for the development of externally validated prognostic models for American visceral leishmaniasis (VL).
The results presented in the systematic review could be useful in identifying patients at higher risk of unfavorable evolution or death from American visceral leishmaniasis (VL).
The results presented in the systematic review might provide an aid in decision-making regarding the clinical management of American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) cases.
There exists a superabundance of human sequence variations.

Testing every sequence variant for association with human disease is often infeasible because studies must be very large and expensive to overcome the statistical penalties used to control for multiple tests.
A common alternative to testing every sequence variant is to assay only a subset of sequence variants for which there are prior reasons to believe they may be disease-causing.
Sequence variants that change conserved amino acids are often disease-causing.
Variants that occur at homologous positions within paralogous human proteins can be used as a means of identifying disease-causing DNA sequence variations.

DNA sequence variants co-occur at aligned amino acid pairs more frequently than expected by chance, suggesting that similar functional constraints on paralogous proteins result in coordinated distributions of variants along their lengths.
If one member of a variant-pair is disease-causing, its partner is likely to be disease-causing as well.
The co-occurrence of disease-causing sequence variants at homologous positions in paralogous proteins provides new avenues for the identification of disease-causing sequence variations.

The human brain is theorised to operate like a sophisticated hypothesis tester, using past experience to generate a model of the external world, testing predictions of this model against incoming sensory evidence, and generating a ‘prediction error’ signal that updates the model when predictions and sensory evidence do not match.
An optimal system should predict the reliability (or ‘precision’) of sensory signals to minimise the influence of unreliable sensory information.
Attention optimises the process of prediction by boosting prediction error signals, which are coded as the difference (or ‘mismatch’) between predicted and observed stimulus features.
The theory predicts that attention should increase the selectivity for mismatch information in the neural response to surprising stimuli.

In a study with human participants, a decoding algorithm was trained to identify ‘mismatch information’ in the brain recorded by electroencephalography (EEG) following the presentation of surprising stimuli that were either attended or ignored.

Attention increased the selectivity for mismatch information in the neural response to surprising stimuli in human participants, supporting the notion that attention and prediction are intricately related processes.
Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is an important cause of neurologic infections in Asia, resulting in substantial disability and deaths.
Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is believed to be endemic in the Philippines.
Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is an important cause of encephalitis and febrile illness in all three major island groups of the Philippines.
The majority of Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) cases in the Philippines were seen in children younger than 15 years.
Males were more often affected than females by Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) in the Philippines.
The national laboratory in the Philippines initiated testing of referred Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) cases in 2009.
Surveillance for acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) with laboratory confirmation of a subset of cases was established in the Philippines in 2011.
From 2011 to 2014, there were 1,032 cases of suspected Japanese encephalitis (JE) in the Philippines.
Of 497 cases with specimens tested from 2011 to 2014 in the Philippines, 73 (15%) had laboratory-confirmed Japanese encephalitis (JE).
Japanese encephalitis (JE) has an extensive geographic distribution in the Philippines.
The findings from the review support the introduction of Japanese encephalitis (JE) vaccine into the Philippines’ routine immunization program.
Human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) is a cellular restriction factor against many viruses.
The role of human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) with regard to the flavivirus family is largely unknown.
Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) was sensitive to human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) in this study.
Dengue virus and Zika virus were resistant to human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) in this study.
Human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) specifically targets Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) viral RNA and induces translation repression and RNA degradation in this study.
The antiviral spectrum of human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) includes a member of the Flavivirus genus as shown by its activity against Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV).

Seasonal influenza A viruses (IAV) cause tens of thousands of deaths and tens of billions of dollars in economic costs every year in the United States alone, despite widespread pre-exposure and vaccination.
Influenza A virus (IAV) persists within the human population by evading herd immunity through the continual accumulation of immune escape substitutions in a process known as antigenic drift.
The specific mechanisms that facilitate influenza A virus (IAV) antigenic drift remain unclear, making it difficult to design more efficacious, escape-proof vaccines.

The researchers used a high-definition population sequencing approach to understand how influenza A virus (IAV) tolerates the accumulation of immune escape substitutions during antigenic drift without losing fitness.
The influenza A virus (IAV) rapidly acquired N-linked glycan structures on the hemagglutinin (HA) protein following escape from a panel of neutralizing antibodies.
Glycosylation of the hemagglutinin (HA) protein alleviated the deleterious effects of immune escape substitutions on interactions with host cell receptors in influenza A virus (IAV).
High-definition virus population sequencing reveals novel viral adaptive mechanisms that facilitate influenza A virus (IAV) immune evasion.
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the major cause of pneumonia and bronchiolitis among infants and children globally.
In the United States, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections lead to 57,000 hospitalizations among young children, especially in those less than one year old.
Despite the development of immunity following respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection during childhood, individuals remain susceptible to RSV upper respiratory tract reinfection.
The current study explored the antibody repertoires following primary respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection and their evolution in adolescents and adults.

Whole genome-fragment phage display libraries (GFPDL) expressing linear and conformational epitopes from respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) fusion protein (F) and attachment protein (G) were used for unbiased epitope profiling of sera prior to and following RSV infection.
Plasmon Surface Resonance (SPR) was used to measure antibody binding to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) fusion protein (F) and attachment protein (G) peptides and proteins.
A steady increase in respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) fusion protein (F) epitope repertoires from young children to adults was observed in this study.
Several novel epitopes were identified in pre-fusion respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) fusion protein (F) and an immunodominant epitope was identified in F0-p27 in this study.
For respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) attachment protein (G), antibody responses were high following RSV infection in children but declined in adults.
This study identified unlinked evolution of anti-fusion protein (anti-F) and anti-attachment protein (anti-G) antibody responses to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
When a species is grown under optimal conditions, the single-knockout of most of its genes is not likely to affect its viability.
The resilience of biological systems to mutations is termed genetic robustness.

The extent of species' genetic robustness reflects both the range of conditions in which the species can survive and the availability of alternative cellular routes compensating for a gene's loss of function.
The authors developed a computational model for estimating the essentiality of metabolic reactions across natural-like environments and applied it to chart species' level of genetic robustness.

Studying robustness across a wide collection of natural-like environments enables stratification, for each species individually, of the extent of environmental-dependent and environmental-independent robustness.
The level of environmental-dependent robustness is associated with the lifestyle of a species, such as being a specialist or a generalist.
The level of environmental-independent robustness is associated with the metabolic production capacities of a species.
Parasitic worms known as helminths represent an important health problem in large parts of Africa, South America, and Asia.
Once helminth larvae enter the body, they head to the gut where they mature into adults and start laying eggs.
In areas with poor sanitation, helminth eggs may get passed on to other individuals.
The immune system sends large numbers of immune cells to the gut to defend the body against helminths, but it usually struggles to eliminate the parasites.
Without deworming medication, helminth infection can last for many years.
Scientists study helminth infections in the laboratory by using worms that naturally infect mice.
It is difficult to extract immune cells from an infected gut because helminth infection creates strong local responses such as intense slime production to try to flush out the worms.

The standard procedure to obtain immune cells from the gut consists of collecting a gut segment and washing it, stripping away the surface layers with chemicals, and using enzymes to digest the tissues which are then filtered to obtain individual cells.
The standard protocol to extract immune cells from the gut is not able to extract cells during helminth infection.
Ferrer-Font et al. methodically refined every step of the immune cell extraction method and succeeded in obtaining millions of immune cells from infected guts.
For the first time, immune cells obtained from infected guts could be studied and identified using a new technology called spectral flow cytometry.

Over 40 immune cell types were followed throughout the course of helminth infection, revealing that many first responder immune cells were recruited to the gut early on when the worms were still larvae.
The first responder immune cells disappeared once the helminth worms developed into adults.
Microscopy confirmed that the first responder immune cells were found around the developing larvae, likely attacking them.
When the adult helminth worms developed, the first responder immune cells were replaced by other immune cells, which also decreased the longer the worms were present in the gut.
The new immune cell extraction process established by Ferrer-Font et al. can be paired with other technologies that reveal which genes are turned on in individual cells.
The new immune cell extraction method could help map out exactly how the body fights helminth infections and how to improve this response.
The new immune cell extraction method could also be useful to extract immune cells from the gut in other challenging scenarios such as food allergies or inflammatory bowel disorders.
DNA replication copies the genetic information contained in a cell's chromosomes.
A ring-like protein complex, cohesin, holds together each pair of newly-replicated chromosomes, known as sister chromatids.

When the cell divides, cohesin is cleaved, allowing sister chromatids to separate so that each daughter cell receives one member of each sister chromatid pair and thereby inherits a full complement of genes.
Defects in the process of cohesin cleavage and sister chromatid separation result in severe developmental abnormalities.
The genes that underlie the process of cohesin cleavage and sister chromatid separation are among the most frequently mutated in cancer.
Cohesin is enriched at centromeres, which are the chromosomal points of attachment to the apparatus called the mitotic spindle that segregates the sister chromatids into the daughter cells.
The protein complex that loads cohesin onto chromosomes determines the preferential localization of cohesin at centromeres.
The two components of the cohesin loading complex, Scc2 and Scc4, associate as a 1:1 pair.
Hinshaw et al. used a technique called X-ray crystallography to determine the structure of Scc4 bound with a large fragment of Scc2.
The structure determined by X-ray crystallography showed that the elongated Scc4 twists around the fragment of Scc2, forming an extended groove.
Scc2 snakes through the Scc4 groove and emerges at both ends.
Hinshaw et al. performed a series of experiments in yeast cells to probe how Scc4 determines the location at which cohesin loads onto chromosomes.
Experiments in yeast cells revealed that a region on the surface of Scc4 targets both Scc4 and Scc2 to centromeres.
The amino-acid sequence of the centromere-targeting patch on the surface of Scc4 is conserved across species.
The mechanism by which Scc4 localizes cohesin to centromeres may be similar in all eukaryotic organisms.
Most animals can respond to injury with some form of tissue regeneration.
In mammals, tissue regeneration is limited to wound healing.
Other vertebrates such as salamanders and zebrafish can regenerate parts of internal organs and even entire appendages.
The planarian, a flatworm, can regenerate its head or tail following amputation and can regenerate a whole animal from just a small body fragment.
Planarians have a complex internal anatomy, which includes muscles, intestines, a system similar to kidneys, and a central nervous system with a brain.
Planarian regeneration proceeds over several days and involves multiple processes, including gene expression, cell division, and cell death.
Planarians activate different responses depending on whether an injury results in significant tissue loss requiring regeneration or if simple wound healing is sufficient.
Gaviño et al. have identified a key mechanism in the initiation of regeneration following tissue loss centered on the gene follistatin, which is expressed following wounding.
When genetic techniques are used to disrupt the expression of follistatin in planarians, regeneration is completely blocked.
The planarian’s ability to routinely replace old cells via a stem-cell mediated mechanism is unaffected when follistatin expression is disrupted.
Follistatin is specifically required for the replacement of cells lost through injury in planarians.
The protein encoded by follistatin likely initiates tissue regeneration upon substantial tissue loss through inhibition of proteins called Activins.
Activin and Follistatin proteins are broadly conserved in evolution and are also expressed in mammals.
A gene is a segment of DNA that usually carries the information required to build a protein, the molecules responsible for most of life’s processes.
A gene's DNA segment is organized in modules, with coding sections separated by portions of non-coding DNA known as introns.
When a gene is turned on, the gene gets faithfully copied into a molecule of pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA), which contains the alternating coding and non-coding modules.
Before pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) can serve as a template to create a protein, the pre-mRNA must be processed and all the introns removed by a structure called the spliceosome.
If the processing of pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) by the spliceosome goes wrong, inaccurate protein templates are produced that may be damaging for the cell.

Spliceosomes are precise molecular scissors that can recognize where a coding module stops and an intron starts, and then make a snip in the pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) to remove the non-coding sequence.
The spliceosome is a complex molecular machine formed of numerous parts, including one known as U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U1 snRNP), that must come together.
When a pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) has several introns, a spliceosome assembles anew for each of the introns.
Braun et al. designed a new method that allows them to tag spliceosomes extracted from a human cell and follow the spliceosomes as they come together.
The experiments by Braun et al. show that spliceosomes working on different introns in the same pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) actually help each other out.
As one spliceosome assembles, this assembly helps the spliceosome that processes the neighboring intron to get built.
The U1 small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (U1 snRNPs) processing nearby introns collaborate to promote the assembly and activity of the spliceosomes.
The teamwork of spliceosomes processing multiple introns is likely important to guarantee that multiple introns are cut out quickly and accurately.
Studying animal behavior can reveal how animals make decisions based on what they sense in their environment.
Measuring animal behavior can be difficult and time-consuming.
Computer programs that measure and analyze animal movement have made studies of animal behavior faster and easier to complete.
Computer programs that measure and analyze animal movement have made more advanced behavioral experiments possible.
More advanced behavioral experiments have yielded new insights about how the brain organizes behavior.
Scientists have started using new machine learning tools called deep neural networks to measure animal behavior.

Deep neural networks learn to measure animal posture, which is the positions of an animal’s body parts in space, directly from real data such as images or videos without being explicitly programmed with instructions to perform the task.
Deep learning algorithms can automatically track the locations of specific animal body parts in videos faster and more accurately than previous techniques.
The ability of deep learning algorithms to learn from images removes the need to attach physical markers to animals, which may alter their natural behavior.
Graving et al. have created a new deep learning toolkit for measuring animal behavior that combines components from previous tools with the latest advances in computer science.
Simple modifications to how the algorithms are trained can greatly improve their performance.

Adding connections between layers, or ‘neurons’, in the deep neural network and training the algorithm to learn the full geometry of the body by drawing lines between body parts both enhance the accuracy of the deep learning toolkit.
The new deep learning toolkit can measure an animal's pose from previously unseen images with high speed and accuracy after being trained on just 100 examples.
Graving et al. tested their model on videos of fruit flies, zebras, and locusts and found that after training, it was able to accurately track the animals’ movements.
The new deep learning toolkit has an easy-to-use software interface and is freely available for other scientists to use and build on.
The new deep learning toolkit may help scientists in many fields including neuroscience and psychology, as well as other computer scientists.
Companies like Google and Apple use similar algorithms to recognize gestures.
Making gesture recognition algorithms faster and more efficient may make them more suitable for mobile devices like smartphones or virtual-reality headsets.
Possible applications of the new deep learning toolkit include diagnosing and tracking injuries or movement-related diseases in humans and livestock.
The retina is the light sensitive tissue at the back of the human eye, and it contains the fovea, the region that provides the clearest vision.
Light must be focused on the retina to create images, a feat achieved by the transparent parts at the front of the eye called the cornea and lens.
The transparent parts at the front of the eye called the cornea and lens are called the optics.
Between birth and adulthood, the distance between the optics and the fovea grows by about seven millimeters.
Cells called cone photoreceptors, which provide light sensitivity, migrate and pack into the fovea between birth and adulthood.
The eye’s optics adjust to maintain a sharp focus between birth and adulthood.
The brain learns how to process inputs from the eyes to generate mental images that realistically correspond to the physical world during eye development.
A growing proportion of the population has eyes that are too long.
In eyes that are too long, the eye’s optics form an image in front of the retina instead of on it for light reflected by far away objects.
Images of distant objects cannot be seen clearly in eyes that are too long, a condition known as myopia or nearsightedness.
Nearsighted people see less clearly than those who do not use glasses, even when given a sharp image to examine at close range.
It has been hypothesized that visual deficits in nearsighted people result from stretching of the retina as the eye becomes bigger.
Testing the hypothesis that retinal stretching causes visual deficits in nearsighted people by looking at cone photoreceptors directly in the eye was impossible until recently.
The optics of all eyes have small imperfections that distort the light passing through them, including any light used to take high resolution microscopic images of the fovea.
Adaptive optics overcomes the hurdle of optical imperfections by adding a deformable mirror to the instrument used to image the eye that can adjust to correct the distortion.
Wang et al. use a new generation Adaptive Optics Scanning Laser Ophthalmoscope to check the density of cones at the fovea in relation to the size of the eye.
Although the center of the fovea has fewer cones when the eye is bigger, this effect is more than offset because the longer eye increases magnification.

A near-sighted person wearing contacts would most likely have more cones sampling the image and should therefore have a higher resolution view than someone who does not need glasses when admiring the full moon side-by-side.
Reductions in the density of cone photoreceptors are ruled out as the cause or effect of visual deficits associated with near-sightedness.
Information stored in DNA is used to make proteins in a two-step process.
In the first step of protein synthesis, the DNA is copied to make molecules of messenger ribonucleic acid (messenger RNA).
Ribosomes use the messenger RNAs as templates to assemble chains of amino acids in a process called translation.
Transfer RNA carries each amino acid to the ribosomes.
If a specific transfer RNA is not available for translation at the right time, the ribosome might stall as it moves along the messenger RNA.
If the ribosome stalls and is not restarted, the ribosome will fall off the messenger RNA without finishing the protein.
Certain types of brain cells are very sensitive to ribosome stalling and tend to die if translation does not continue.
A protein called GTPBP2 plays an important role in restarting stalled ribosomes in certain brain cells.
Ribosome stalling activates an enzyme known as GCN2 in brain cells of mutant mice that lacked the GTPBP2 protein.
GCN2 triggers stress responses in brain cells by activating a communication system called the ATF4 pathway.
The ATF4 pathway protects brain cells from damage, and the absence of the ATF4 pathway results in more rapid cell deterioration and death.
Organs begin developing during the first few months of pregnancy while the baby is still an embryo.
Embryogenesis is a tightly organized process during which the embryo forms different layers of stem cells.
The layers of stem cells formed during embryogenesis can be activated to turn into a particular type of cell, such as a heart or a lung cell.
The heart and lungs develop from different layers within the embryo, which must communicate with each other for the organs to form correctly.
Chemical signals can be released from and travel between layers of the embryo, activating processes inside cells located in the different areas.
In mouse models, chemical signals and cells travel between developing heart and lung, which helps both organs to form into the correct structure.
It is unclear how well the observations from mouse models translate to heart and lung development in humans.
Ng et al. developed a human model of heart and lung co-development during embryogenesis using human pluripotent stem cells.
The laboratory-grown human pluripotent stem cells were treated with chemical signals, causing them to form different layers that developed into early forms of heart and lung cells.
The human pluripotent stem cells were transferred into a specific growing condition where they arranged into three-dimensional structures termed microtissues.
Lung cells developed faster when grown in microtissues with accompanying developing heart cells compared to microtissues containing only developing lung cells in the human model.
The co-developing heart and lung tissues automatically separate from each other during later stages without the need for chemical signals in the human model.

This human cell-based model of early forms of co-developing heart and lung cells may help provide researchers with new strategies to probe the underlying mechanisms of human heart and lung interaction during embryogenesis.
Cells with complex interlocking shapes, similar to pieces of a jigsaw puzzle, cover the surface of many leaves.
Plant cells are like small balloons surrounded by a strong cell wall.
The internal pressure inside plant cells can be higher than the pressure in a car tire.
The internal pressure inside plant cells gives non-woody plant tissue its shape.
Removing the internal pressure inside plant cells causes the plant to wilt.
The pressure inside a plant cell creates a lot of mechanical stress on the epidermal cell walls that make up the surface of the plant.
The extent of mechanical stress on epidermal cell walls depends on the shape and size of the cells.
Large plant cells bulge out and experience more mechanical stress than small plant cells.
The shape of puzzle cells is an adaptation used by plants to reduce the stress on their surface.
Sapala, Runions et al. developed a computer simulation that models how a plant grows and re-creates a variety of realistic puzzle cell shapes.
The simulations show that paving the leaf surface with puzzle shaped cells instead of more regularly shaped cells reduces the stress in the epidermal cell walls.
The simulations show that complex puzzle shapes develop in parts of the plant that grow isotropically, such as leaves.
If a plant organ grows mostly in one direction, like in a root or stem, long thin cells are sufficient to reduce the stress on the epidermal cell wall.

Sapala, Runions et al. tested the idea that puzzle cell shape is related to organ shape and growth direction by analyzing the shape of organs and cells in many plant species and by genetically modifying growth directions in Arabidopsis thaliana plants.
The analysis confirmed that puzzle cell shape is related to both organ shape and how isotropically the plant grows.
It had previously been proposed that mobile chemical signals passed between cells coordinate the process by which a lobe in one puzzle cell matches an indentation in its neighbor.
The model developed by Sapala, Runions et al. does not require chemical signaling to explain puzzle cell shape formation.
Mechanical forces and the shape of the puzzle cells themselves may transmit information coordinating puzzle cell shape.
Mechanical forces have important effects on the shape and behavior of cells from other species.
Animal cells can develop into different cell types depending on the stiffness of the surface they are placed on.
Sapala, Runions et al. have highlighted that plant cell shapes also adapt to mechanical forces.
Many species, including humans, use social interaction to reduce the effects of stress.
The lack of a social network may itself be a source of stress.
Recent research suggests that young girls are more sensitive to social stress than boys.
Social networks may be more important for females in general, and young females from different species, such as mice, may be more sensitive to social isolation than males.
Few studies have examined how social isolation affects the brain cells that control the release of stress hormones.
It remains unknown whether isolating individuals from their social group impacts the brain in sex-specific ways.
The brains of young male and female mice react differently to social isolation.
Less than a day after separation from their littermates, the activity in the brain cells of female mice became markedly different from that of isolated male mice.
The physical stress of being made to swim produced similar changes in the brains of both male and female mice.
The changes in the brain cells that control the release of stress hormones required a signalling chemical called corticosterone, which is produced in response to stressful situations.
In response to social isolation, female mice are experiencing more stress than male mice.
